newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks end sharply lower as rate fears hit Dow.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks end sharply lower as rate fears hit Dow.

text.p: Britain's FTSE 100 index suffered its biggest one-day fall in points of the year so far on Thursday as Wall Street dropped on renewed fears of an imminent rise in U.S. interest rates.

Markets in Europe and the U.S., already weighed down by fears of tighter credit, took fright in early afternoon as comments from the head of the U.S. central bank were taken as a signal of a rate hike as early as next week.
The FTSE 100 index closed 74.1 points lower at 4,258.1, its biggest loss since an 88-point tumble last December -- also prompted by comments from Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan.

Greenspan, who last December warned over "irrational exuberance" in stock markets, said today that the U.S. must act pre-emptively to keep inflation low -- taken as signalling a rate rise at a key policy meeting next week.

Banks and other rate-sensitive financial stocks suffered the brunt of the declines, with Lloyds TSB down 23-1/2p or 4.7 percent at 475-1/2, Barclays off 45p or 3.9 percent at 10.31-1/2 stg and Legal & General -- biggest faller in the FTSE 100 -- down 23-1/2p or 5.8 percent at 384-1/2.
Strategists said UK shares could come under further pressure in the short term at least.
Andy Hartwill, stock market strategist at brokerage SocGen, said the FTSE 100 could drop as low as 4,150 in the short term -- some seven percent below its record 4,466.3 set on March 11.

"The possibility of an interest rate hike is exposing high stock market valuations in the UK and the United States," Hartwill said. "But I would be happy to buy the market not far below its current level."

The SocGen strategist said a modest tightening of credit in coming months could avert an inflationary upturn in the economy, prolonging the steady growth, low inflation background in which markets have flourished in recent months.
"If we get a 75 or 100 basis point tightening over the next 12 months, in the end that is not a significant tightening, but the risks short term are on the downside," Hartwill said.

As Germany's DAX index dropped 1.5 percent, Scott Evans, strategist at UBS, said a correction in markets across Europe had been expected after sharp gains in leading indexes in the early weeks of the year.

Evans pointed out that worry over progress towards monetary union was another negative for European equities, while British shares were also dogged by political uncertainties at the start of a lengthy six-week election campaign.

"All our year-end targets for the FTSE and European indexes were passed about a month ago and it could be a little while before markets start to claw their way back," Evans said. "Short term the outlook is grim."
Trading volume in UK shares was the heaviest for weeks, reaching 1.1 billion shares by 1714 GMT.
Other leading UK indexes also fell with the FTSE 250 mid-range index down 1.9 percent and the Reuters HSBC index of the top 150 shares down 1.7 percent.
The March long gilt contract was down 3/8 at 109-15/32.

"It has been a pretty difficult day," said one share trader. "There are a lot of nervous people out there and it is looking very much like we have seen the top of the market short-term... People have been trying to get out of certain shares and finding there's no market."
A lower-than-expected UK inflation figure for February briefly lifted the FTSE off its lows but was not enough to stop investors fretting about UK interest rates, dealers said.
"Interest rates ought to go up now and whoever wins the election is going to have to put them up. The only question is how much," said another dealer.
Elsewhere the company results season continued with Guinness up 17-1/2p at 503-1/2 as results in line with expectations were accompanied by a positive trading statement.
Supermarket stocks rose after William Morrison Supermarkets results topped expectations and Kleinwort Benson upgraded Tesco, up 5p at 339, to "hold."

Telecoms equipment firm Telspec rose 30p to 227-1/2 as a drop in profits was offset by an upbeat statement from the company promising a recovery in 1997, while P&O dropped 27-1/2p to 630-1/2 after its Dutch container shipping partner announed a 54 percent decline in net profit.
-- David Holmes, London newsroom +44 171 542 4367
